title: Chapter 62: Sola's Grandchildren, Part 1 of 5: Leaving Thistle Ford
html:
Lyra counted the steps out of Thistle Ford because her father was being buried tomorrow, and counting was the only thing she knew how to do with her hands.
One, down the ladder from the loft. Two, three, four, across the byre, past the two brown cows, who turned their heads and watched her go with their wet, patient eyes. Five, the step down into the yard. Then the yard itself, white and hard with frost, and her boots crunching on it, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and the cold so sharp after the warm straw that it made her eyes water.
It was just after dawn. The sky over the hills was the color of a pigeon's breast, gray going to pink at the edges, and the air was so still that the smoke from the chimneys of Thistle Ford went straight up in thin blue lines and did not bend at all. Somewhere a cock was crowing. Somewhere a door banged. The river was talking to itself over its stones, the same as last night, as if it had not stopped once in the dark.
She had slept. That surprised her. She had lain down in the straw under the little frosted window with her back to Corin, sure that she would lie awake all night thinking about tomorrow, and the next thing she knew, the window was gray and Oren was snoring and the cows were moving below. She did not remember dreaming. She was not sure, now, whether she was glad of that or not.
Corin had been awake before her. She had seen that as soon as she opened her eyes. He was sitting against the post in the middle of the loft with the green book open on his knee, reading the first page. His lips were moving a little as he read. She had lain very still and watched him do it, through her lashes, the way she had watched him every morning in the crypt, and she had seen the moment when he came to the line about her, and stopped, and read it again.
Then he had shut the book, and looked across at her, and she had shut her eyes.
She did not know why she did that. She did it every morning. As if it would be worse, somehow, for him to know that she had seen him learn who she was.
Now she stood in the frosty yard and counted, and waited for the others.
Granny Abbe was already up. Of course she was. She came round the corner of the hall with her army coat flapping round her ankles and her cold pipe in her mouth, and Hild behind her carrying a bundle. The bundle was a cloth tied up at the corners. Hild put it into Lyra's arms without a word, and Lyra felt the weight of it, and the shapes inside.
"Apples," said Granny Abbe. "The dried ones. And a cheese. And oatcake. It'll not go far, but it'll go further than nothing." She looked Lyra up and down with her small black eyes. "You'll want your hands free on the hill. Put it in his pack. The big one's."
"Thank you," said Lyra.
The old woman waved this away, the way you wave away a fly.
"Davin's coming," she said. "He'll take you to Haverstock, and past it, to the Lip. Then he'll come home." She took the pipe out of her mouth and pointed it at Lyra, like a finger. "He'll come home. You hear me? You'll not take him past the last cairn."
"No," said Lyra. "We won't."
"Good." The pipe went back in. Granny Abbe looked past her, at the ladder in the byre door, where Oren was coming down backward, slowly, one-handed, with his sling held against his chest. And then at the ladder again, where Corin was coming after him, even more slowly, with Hild's hand ready under his elbow.
The old woman watched him all the way down. She watched him find his crutch. She watched him step out into the frosty yard and lift his face and turn it, very slightly, toward the north, the way a plant turns toward a window.
Lyra saw her watch. She saw something come into the old brown face, and then go out of it again.
"Granny Abbe," said Lyra, before she could stop herself.
"Aye?"
"Last night. You said—" She stopped. She had not meant to say anything. She did not know what she had meant to say. You said the dolls were for the children who go over the glass. You said nobody goes north of here now. You said it as if somebody once did. "Nothing," she said. "Thank you. For the loft."
Granny Abbe looked at her for a long moment.
"Ask at Last Thorn," she said. Just that.
Then a dog barked, once, at the end of the street, and a small figure came up out of the river mist with a long crooked stick and a black-and-white shadow running at its heels.
It was the boy from the ridge. Lyra saw him properly now for the first time. He was small and thin and very solemn, with a face so freckled that it looked as if someone had flicked a brush of brown paint at it, and hair the color of straw sticking out from under a knitted cap. He wore a coat that had been a man's coat, cut down, with the sleeves rolled. His stick was taller than he was. His dog was a lean, quick, silent thing, with one blue eye and one brown, and it went straight to Oren and sniffed his boots and then sat down on them.
Oren looked down at it.
"Well," he said. "Good morning to you."
The dog thumped its tail on the frost.
"That's Flint," said the boy. He did not look at any of them. He looked at the ground about a yard in front of his own feet. "He likes you. He doesn't like anybody." He turned and started walking up the street toward the hill, without waiting to see if they followed. Over his shoulder he said, "Granny says Haverstock. Come on, then."
They came on.
Lyra counted. Eleven. Twelve. Thirteen. Past the hall, with its worn carved sun on the door. Fourteen, fifteen. Past the last house, where a woman was standing in her doorway with a baby on her hip, watching them go. Sixteen. Seventeen. Onto the road that went up out of the valley, between its two low walls, toward the north.
She looked back, once, at the eighteenth step.
Granny Abbe was still standing in the frosty yard in front of the byre, very small, with her hands in the sleeves of her army coat and her cold pipe in her mouth. She was not watching Lyra. She was not watching Oren, or the boy, or the dog.
She was watching Corin's back, going up the hill.
Lyra turned round again, and kept counting.
Tomorrow
The road out of Thistle Ford went up the side of the valley in long, easy bends, and the snow on it had been trodden down by the village's sheep and carts, so that the walking was easy. Too easy. When the walking was hard, Lyra did not have to think. When it was easy, she thought.
She thought about tomorrow.
Tomorrow was Sunday. Tomorrow, at the second bell after noon, they would carry her father into Saint Clement's.
She knew exactly how it would be. She had been to Saint Clement's a hundred times. It was the Thorne church, the church on the Hill where all the Thornes had been christened and married and buried for longer than anyone could remember, and she knew every stone of it. The white steps. The squat square tower. The bell, which was cracked, and had been cracked since her grandfather's day, so that it did not ring so much as clank, a deep flat sad sound like somebody dropping a pan. The saints painted on the walls inside, with their gold rings round their heads, faded to the color of old butter. The smell of cold wax.
And under the church, down a narrow stair, the vault. The Thorne vault. Low arches, stone shelves, and on the shelves the long boxes. Her grandfather. Her grandmother. Great-uncles she had never met. And on one shelf, near the end, a box with her mother's name on it.
They would put her father beside her mother.
She would not be there.
Rowan would be there. Rowan, in his cadet's black, standing very straight, with his face shut like a door. Aunt Cressida would be there, in a veil, smelling of lilies. The Duke, perhaps. Bertram, the old butler, who had been with them since before she was born, and who would cry, and pretend he was not crying. Mrs. Doyle, perhaps, from Saint Bride's, with her candles. Kross. Almost certainly Kross.
And she would be here. On a road in the snow, in a boy's breeches and a dead man's coat, walking the other way.
She had chosen it. She knew she had chosen it. Her father had died on Thursday afternoon with his closed hand under hers, and on Thursday night she had changed her clothes and given her mother's gown to Mrs. Doyle and walked out of the city with Corin, because Kross had said be gone by then, and because Corin's name was on a list, and because she had written in his book, with her own blood, that she was coming after.
She had chosen it. That did not make it easier. If anything, it made it worse.
Forty, she counted. Forty-one. Forty-two.
They stopped to rest at the top of the first long rise, where the road came out of the valley onto a broad, bare shoulder of hill, white and empty, with the sky very big above it. Davin sat down on the wall with his stick across his knees and did not look at anyone. Flint lay down at Oren's feet. Oren eased the strap of his sling and looked north.
Corin sat on the wall a little way along and took out the green book.
Lyra did not mean to look. She was standing behind him, a little to one side, and she meant to look at the view. But the book was open on his knee, and his head was bent over it, and the pencil was in his fist, and she could see the page past his shoulder.
She could see her own words.
Not her own hand. Never again her own hand. His hand, his square crooked capitals, so crooked now that some of the letters leaned against each other like drunk men. But her words. Things she had said yesterday, on the road.
IT WAS A JUG. BLUE AND WHITE. HE PUT HIS HAND ON HER FATHER.
And under it, a little further down:
SHE BREAKS BREAD LIKE SOMEBODY WHO HAS DONE IT BEFORE.
And under that:
I THINK SHE HAS DONE IT BEFORE. FOR ME.
She stood very still.
She had done it before. Many times. On the barge, when his hands first started going gray and the cold got into them. In the crypt, when he had the fever. She had broken his bread for him and dipped it in his soup and put it in his hand, and he had not even noticed, most of the time, because he was talking, or thinking, or arguing with the old man in his head. She had done it so often that her hands did it by themselves now. That was why she had done it yesterday, without thinking. Her hands remembered him, even if he did not remember her.
And he had seen. And he had guessed. FOR ME.
She wanted, suddenly and very badly, to take the pencil out of his hand and write something under it.
She did not know what. Yes. Or You were always too busy talking to notice. Or You used to say thank you with your mouth full. Something. Anything. A line of her own under his, in her own quick hand, the way she used to, the way the old Ledger was full of her quick hand all through, arguing with him in the margins.
She reached out.
She did not touch the pencil. She did not have to. She knew what would happen if she did. She had tried, on Wednesday, on the steps of Saint Bride's, and again on Thursday night in the crypt, when nobody was looking, with a stub of Gideon's chalk on the floor. She had held the chalk the way she had held a pen all her life, and thought of the letter L, the easiest letter, the first letter of her own name. Two lines. Down, and across.
And her hand had made a mark like a beetle walking. A wandering, shaking line that went nowhere and meant nothing. And she had sat on the cold floor of the crypt and looked at it, and understood, really understood for the first time, that it was gone. Not hidden. Not hurt. Gone, the way a word goes out of a room when you shut the door on it. She had paid it away, folding the square into her father's hand. She had paid with the hand she would have used to unfold it. That was the rule.
She took her hand back. She put both hands deep in the sleeves of Silas's coat, where nobody could see them.
Corin had not noticed. He was writing something new, slowly, at the bottom of the page. She did not read it. She turned away and looked at the view, the way she had meant to in the first place, and the view was very wide and very white and very empty, and she looked at it until her eyes stung, and told herself it was the wind.
Fifty, she counted, though she was not walking. Fifty-one.
She still had four. That was what she thought about, standing there with her hands hidden. Four memories of her mother, left, out of five. The hair brushing: a hundred strokes, every night, and her mother counting them in a language Lyra did not know. The rain on Crown Walk, and her father's voice: Isolde, you'll catch your death. The empty chair at Midwinter. And the song. The song that went up, and hung, and came down, and came home.
She had given the fifth to the Duke, for a card with his name on it. Her mother in a traveling cloak, in the front hall, holding Lyra's face in two gray gloves, and then a carriage, and never coming back. She did not have that one anymore. She knew she had had it, the way you know you had a coin because there is a hole in your pocket the size of it.
Four left. And her father's hand, closed, going down into the dark tomorrow with the last thing she had ever written folded up inside it.
"Lyra."
She turned.
Corin had shut the book. He was looking up at her from the wall, with his gray face lifted, and his eyes were careful on her face.
"Are you all right?"
She thought about lying.
Then she thought about the page. Rule one. He had read it every morning since Thursday. It was in his own hand, and he believed it, because he had nothing else to believe.
"No," she said. "Not today. Tomorrow's the funeral."
He did not say he was sorry. He did not say anything for a while. Then he nodded, slowly, and moved along the wall a little, so that there was room beside him.
She did not sit down. But she stood a little closer, after that, until Oren said it was time to go.
The General
The children found them a mile out of Thistle Ford.
Lyra did not see where they came from. One moment the road ahead was empty, a gray trodden line between two white walls, and the next there were four of them, sitting in a row on the top of the left-hand wall like birds on a fence, swinging their legs. Three boys and a girl. The girl was the biggest. She had a red knitted cap pulled down over her ears and a face so round and so cold-pink that she looked like an apple.
"That's Wenna," said Davin, without looking up. "And her brothers. They followed us."
"We didn't follow you," said the girl called Wenna. "We were here first."
"You followed us round by the top field. I saw you."
"Did not."
Davin did not argue. He walked past them with his stick and his dog, looking at the road a yard in front of his feet. The four children jumped down off the wall, one after another, thump thump thump thump into the snow, and fell in behind him. Not behind Davin. Behind Oren.
They walked behind Oren in a row, close, the way ducklings walk behind a duck, and looked up at him.
Oren walked faster. They walked faster.
Oren slowed down. They slowed down.
At last he stopped and turned round and looked down at them, a big gray-bearded man with his arm in a flour-sack sling and a sword on his hip, and the four of them stopped too, all at once, and looked back up at him with their mouths a little open.
"Well?" said Oren. "What is it?"
Nobody answered. Then the smallest boy, who could not have been more than five, said in a high clear voice, "Are you the General's?"
Oren looked at him.
"The what?"
"The General's." The boy pointed at him with a mittened hand. "Mam says you're the General's. Mam says you've come back."
Wenna hit him on the back of the head, not hard. "You don't say it. Granny Abbe said not to say it."
"I didn't say it to Granny Abbe. I said it to him."
Oren looked at Lyra over the children's heads. His face was the face of a man who has walked into a room in the dark and found it full of furniture. She did not know what to tell him. She shook her head very slightly.
Oren looked back down at the boy.
"What general?" he said carefully.
The four children stared at him.
It was a very particular stare. Lyra knew it. It was the stare that children give a grown-up who has asked a question so stupid that it must be a trick. What is water? What is the sky?
"The General," said Wenna slowly, as if to somebody simple. "Sola. The General. Who made the Glass."
The road went quiet.
Corin had stopped a little way behind, leaning on his crutch. Lyra saw his face change at the name. She saw him look north, past the children, past the walls, to where the white hills went up and up toward the sky.
Oren said nothing at all.
"She was a Vance," said Wenna. She said it as if it were the beginning of a story she had heard so many times she could say it in her sleep. "Sola Vance. She lived at Haverstock, at the top house, where the smith is now. And when them in the gray came up the valleys with their lamps, she went down to the valley to stop them, and everybody went with her. And she said—" Wenna stopped. Her round face went solemn. "She didn't say. She couldn't. She'd given all her words away. That's how she did it. She gave all her words away, every single one, and it made the sun come out of her, and the sun burned them in the gray all up, and it made the Glass." She took a breath. "And then she was gone too. And all of them that went with her. And that's why we don't burn, up here. Because she burned enough for everybody."
The smallest boy nodded hard all the way through this, as if he were helping.
"And now," said Wenna, "you've come back."
She looked at Oren with her round pink face, completely certain.
Oren opened his mouth. He shut it again. Lyra saw his good hand close and open at his side, the way it did when he was reaching for a word, and could not find it, and did not know whether it was because the word was gone or because there was no word for this at all.
"I'm a soldier," he said at last. "From the city. I'm nobody's."
"You're a Vance," said Wenna.
"Lots of folk are called Vance."
"Not up here," said Wenna. "Up here there's only the stone."
She did not explain what she meant. She seemed to think she did not need to. She turned round, and her three brothers turned round with her, and they all went running back down the road toward Thistle Ford, kicking up the snow, shouting something to each other that the wind took away.
At the bend, the smallest boy stopped and turned and waved. Then he ran after the others.
Oren stood in the road and watched them go.
"Saints," he said quietly. "Saints and all their candles."
Lyra came up beside him. She did not know what to say, so she did not say anything. She put her hand on his good arm, the way she had in the hall, and left it there.
"My grandfather," said Oren, after a while. He was still looking down the road. "My father's father. He came to the city from somewhere north. I never knew where. He never said. He'd never talk about it. He used to say there was nothing up north but sheep and weather and a long walk back." He was quiet. "I used to think that was a joke."
"Maybe it was," said Lyra.
"Maybe." Oren rubbed his beard. "He had a word. When things went wrong. When the bread burned or a horse threw a shoe. He'd say it under his breath. I never knew what it meant. It wasn't a city word." He frowned. "I can't remember it now. I don't know if that's because I've lost it, or because I never had it right." He shook his head. "Saints. I'm a soldier. I'm nobody's."
Davin had not stopped. He was a long way up the road now, a small dark figure with a stick, and the dog trotting at his heels. He did not look back.
"Come on," said Lyra. "He won't wait."
They went on up the road toward Haverstock. Behind them, Corin came more slowly, on his crutch, looking north.
